{{italic title}}

{{Infobox book
| image             = Georg Mohr's Euclides Danicus, Cover.png

'''''Euclides Danicus''''' ({{Literal translation|Danish Euclid}}) is one of three books of mathematics written by [[Georg Mohr]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Andersen | first1 = Kirsti
 | last2 = Meyer | first2 = Henrik
 | doi = 10.1111/j.1600-0498.1985.tb00833.x
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Centaurus
 | mr = 825846
 | pages = 139–144
 | title = Georg Mohr's three books and the ''Gegenübung auf Compendium Euclidis Curiosi''
 | volume = 28
 | year = 1985| bibcode = 1985Cent...28..139A
 }}.</ref> It was published in 1672 simultaneously in [[Copenhagen]] and [[Amsterdam]], in [[Danish language|Danish]] and [[Dutch language|Dutch]] respectively. It contains the first proof of the [[Mohr–Mascheroni theorem]], which states that every geometric construction that can be performed using a [[compass and straightedge]] can also be done with compass alone.<ref name="gla">{{citation
 | last = Alexanderson | first = Gerald L. | authorlink = Gerald L. Alexanderson
 | date = July 2014
 | doi = 10.1090/S0273-0979-2014-01458-2
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society
 | pages = 463–467
 | title = About the cover: Two theorems on geometric constructions
 | volume = 51| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

==Contents==
The book is divided into two parts. In the first part, Mohr shows how to perform all of the constructions of [[Euclid]]'s [[Euclid's Elements|''Elements'']] using a compass alone. In the second part, he includes some other specific constructions, including some related to the mathematics of the [[sundial]].<ref>{{citation|title=An Impression of Mathematics in Denmark in the Period 1600–1800|first=Kirsti|last=Andersen|doi=10.1111/j.1600-0498.1980.tb00381.x|journal=Centaurus|volume=24|issue=1|year=1980|pages=316–334|bibcode=1980Cent...24..316A }}.</ref>

==1928 rediscovery of the book==
''Euclides Danicus'' languished in obscurity, possibly caused by its choice of language, until its rediscovery in 1928 in a bookshop in Copenhagen. Until then, the Mohr–Mascheroni theorem had been credited to [[Lorenzo Mascheroni]], who published a proof in 1797, independently of Mohr's work.<ref name="gla"/><ref name="nac"/> Soon after the rediscovery of Mohr's book, publications about it by [[Florian Cajori]] and [[Nathan Altshiller Court]] made its existence much more widely known.<ref name="gla"/><ref name="nac">{{citation
 | last = Court | first = N. A. | authorlink = Nathan Altshiller Court
 | doi = 10.1090/S0002-9904-1930-04976-9
 | issue = 7
 | journal = Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 1561975
 | page = 471
 | title = Book Review: Euclides Danicus
 | volume = 36
 | year = 1930| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Cajori | first = Florian | authorlink = Florian Cajori
 | doi = 10.2307/2298942
 | issue = 7
 | journal = [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | mr = 1521787
 | pages = 364–365
 | title = A Forerunner of Mascheroni
 | volume = 36
 | year = 1929| jstor = 2298942 }}.</ref> The Danish version was republished in facsimile in 1928 by the [[Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters]], with a foreword by [[Johannes Hjelmslev]],<ref name="gla"/><ref name="nac"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Menger | authorlink = Karl Menger
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01696783
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik
 | language = German
 | mr = 1549801
 | page = A3
 | title = Literaturberichte: Euclides Danicus
 | volume = 37
 | year = 1930| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=''Euclides danicus'', Amsterdam 1672 by Georg Mohr; Johannes Hjelmslev; ''Beiträge zur Lebensbeschreibung von Georg Mohr'' (1640-1697) by Johannes Hjelmslev|first=George|last=Sarton|authorlink=George Sarton|journal=[[Isis (journal)|Isis]]|volume=26|issue=1|year=1936|pages=167–170|jstor= 225067|doi=10.1086/347140}}.</ref> and a [[German language|German]] translation was published in 1929.<ref name="gla"/>

==Surviving copies==
Only eight copies of the original publication of the book are known to survive. In 2005, one of these original copies was sold at auction, to [[Fry's Electronics]], for what [[Gerald L. Alexanderson]] calls a "ridiculously low price": US$13,000.<ref name="gla"/>
